questions.prompt: What is the balance factor of a node in an AVL tree, and what range keeps the tree balanced?

options.text: The colour of the node, kept red or black
Number of nodes on the left minus on the right, kept in {-1, 0, +1}
Depth of the node, kept below log n
Height of left subtree minus height of right subtree, kept in {-1, 0, +1}

questions.explanation: AVL balance is defined by subtree heights, and any node whose factor leaves {-1, 0, +1} triggers a rotation. This keeps the height within about 1.44 log n.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum number of rotations needed to rebalance an AVL tree after a single insertion?
questions.explanation: One insertion unbalances at most one node critically, and a single or double rotation there restores the whole tree. Deletion, by contrast, may require rotations up the whole path.

questions.prompt: A red-black tree guarantees what bound on its height for n nodes?
questions.explanation: The red-black invariants ensure no root-to-leaf path is more than twice any other, bounding height at 2 log(n+1). This gives O(log n) operations with fewer rotations than AVL on updates.

questions.prompt: Why are B-trees preferred over binary search trees for on-disk database indexes?

options.text: They use less memory per key
They keep keys unsorted for faster insertion
High fan-out makes the tree shallow, minimising expensive disk reads

questions.explanation: A B-tree node holds many keys and fills a disk block, so the tree is only a few levels deep. Since each level costs a disk seek, a shallow high-fan-out tree dramatically cuts I/O.

questions.prompt: How does a B+ tree differ from a B-tree?

options.text: It is always a binary tree
All data pointers live in the leaves, which are linked for range scans
It stores at most two keys per node
It cannot be used on disk

questions.explanation: In a B+ tree the internal nodes hold only separator keys for routing, and every record pointer sits in a leaf. The linked leaves make ordered range queries a simple leaf traversal.

questions.prompt: What is the practical trade-off between an AVL tree and a red-black tree?

options.text: Red-black trees do not support ordered traversal
AVL is more rigidly balanced, so faster lookups but more rotations on updates
Red-black trees are always shorter than AVL trees

questions.explanation: AVL's tighter height limit favours read-heavy workloads, while red-black trees do less restructuring per update and suit write-heavy use, which is why many library maps use them.

questions.prompt: In a B-tree of order m, how many children can an internal node have at most?
questions.explanation: Order m means up to m children and therefore up to m - 1 keys per node. A non-root node must be at least half full to keep the tree balanced.

questions.prompt: An LL imbalance in an AVL tree (a node heavy on its left child's left subtree) is fixed by:
questions.explanation: A left-left case is resolved by one right rotation about the unbalanced node. The zig-zag cases (LR and RL) need a double rotation; recolouring belongs to red-black trees.

questions.prompt: What is the height of an AVL tree with n nodes, asymptotically?
questions.explanation: The minimum node count for height h follows a Fibonacci recurrence, which grows exponentially, so height is logarithmic in n. This guarantees O(log n) search, insert and delete.

questions.prompt: Which property must every root-to-leaf path in a red-black tree satisfy?

options.text: It contains the same number of red nodes
It contains the same number of black nodes
It has exactly log n nodes
It alternates strictly red and black

questions.explanation: Equal black-height on every path, combined with the rule that a red node cannot have a red child, is what bounds the longest path at twice the shortest and keeps the tree balanced.
